compression.title: Amiel Melburn Trust Archive
compression.lede: is the Barry Amiel and Norman Melburn Trust's online database of socialist and radical writings: thirteen British periodicals and series from 1956, beginning with The Reasoner and the New Reasoner, the journals E.P. Thompson and John Saville kept after the Communist Party of Great Britain ordered The Reasoner closed (the archive; maryleelabor record; #1725).

sentences.text: The Amiel Melburn Trust Archive (banmarchive.org.uk) is, in its About page's words, "an indexed and searchable online database of socialist and radical writings", and on its home page "an online database of socialist and radical writings" (banmarchive.org.uk), the kind under which the maryleelabor census record enters it and asks of it the census's question: "Whose record does it keep, who holds it, and does it keep the losing side in a form that could be taken up later?" (maryleelabor record).

Its own page titles read "Amiel Melburn Trust Archive - Amiel Melburne Trust Archive" (banmarchive.org.uk), and the record gives Amiel Melburn Archive, Amiel Melburne Trust Archive and banmarchive as its other names, places it in two of the census's six areas, movement documents and archives and custody, and gives periodical runs and movement documents as its kinds of evidence (maryleelabor record).

It is the Barry Amiel and Norman Melburn Trust's: its pages carry "© Barry Amiel and Norman Melburn Trust" and "Registered Charity No. 281239", link to the Trust's website and its lectures, and call the Trust "a non-profit charitable organisation" (banmarchive.org.uk), and the Trust's site lists it as its "Online library", the "Amiel & Melburn Trust Internet Archive" (amielandmelburn.org.uk).

The record names the operator as the Trust, "Registered Charity No. 281239, London; site by Common Knowledge", and the holder as "a registered charity" whose "terms of use and license" are "not stated on the saved pages" (maryleelabor record).

The archive's pages give the Trust's address as PO Box 80552, London SE4 9FH (banmarchive.org.uk), and the Trust's own site, its footer dated 2015, gives PO Box 79650, London SE8 9BT, under the same charity number (amielandmelburn.org.uk).

"The Trust was founded in 1980 by Norman Melburn and named for his friend and fellow Marxist, the lawyer Barry Amiel", and since Melburn's death in 1991 both men have been commemorated in its name (amielandmelburn.org.uk).

Its objectives are "to advance public education, learning and knowledge in all aspects of the philosophy of Marxism, the history of socialism, and the working class movement"; it initiates activity and research and gives financial assistance to bodies or individuals for projects within its remit (amielandmelburn.org.uk), which Bath and North East Somerset Council's funding finder gives as project grants of up to £15,750 to UK charitable organisations and individuals (bathnes.gov.uk).

The council's page sets out Regular Awards up to £7,350, Major Awards above £7,350 and up to £15,750 considered once a year, and Urgent Small Awards up to £500; an aim to ringfence half of the funds for popular political education reaching non-academic and non-activist audiences; no grants for core costs; and applications normally opened in May and November (bathnes.gov.uk).

Among the projects funded before, the same page lists "The maintenance of libraries and archive material" (bathnes.gov.uk), and the Trust's awards page shows ten awards of 2025 from £3,500 to £15,248, among them political education for on-demand food delivery riders and "an open-access archive of materials from peace movements" (amielandmelburn.org.uk).

Its news pages record a Trust-funded comic-book people's history of occupations in Scotland, an annual research fellowship "to facilitate research with a socialist orientation" held with a partner organisation, in 2022–23 the Independent Workers' union of Great Britain, a 140-page report on political education made with The World Transformed, and an annual lecture by Jodi Dean in 2022 (amielandmelburn.org.uk).

The archive lists thirteen publications, from The Reasoner (3 issues, 1956) and the Socialist History Society Pamphlets (38 issues, 1956–1976) through Marxism Today (145 issues, 1978–1998) to New University (13 issues, 1960–2024) (banmarchive.org.uk), which the record sums as "13 publications, 335 issues", lists title by title, and gives as covering Britain from "1956 (The Reasoner) to 2024 (New University, as listed)" (maryleelabor record).

The About page counts "more than 2,500 articles", most in PDF, "which has allowed for the preservation of the original look and typesetting" (banmarchive.org.uk), and Common Knowledge describes "almost 70 years of radical writing, including writings by Stuart Hall and E.P. and Dorothy Thompson" (commonknowledge.coop).

Common Knowledge reads the titles one by one, Red Rag for "the richness of feminist history", Race & Class on interacting forms of oppression, Black Dwarf "from the heady days of the late 1960s", and "the whole archive of the influential Marxism Today" with its "often controversial 'New Times' hypothesis" (commonknowledge.coop), and the record names its object as "thirteen British socialist and radical periodicals and series, 1956 onward" (maryleelabor record).

The archive's New Reasoner page gives the origin of its first titles: "When E.P. Thompson and John Saville were instructed by the leadership of the Communist Party of Great Britain to close down their journal The Reasoner , which had been critical of what the editors saw as the Party’s dogmatism, they refused." (banmarchive.org.uk).

Suspended from the party, they "soon resigned in protest at the Soviet invasion of Hungary" and relaunched with the New Reasoner, which "urged a reconsideration of the longer traditions of radical politics" and laid the basis of Thompson's humanist socialism (banmarchive.org.uk); #1725 gives the same case from Saville's 1976 account, in which the journal "opened discussion inside the Communist Party of Great Britain after the Twentieth Congress", the party demanded they stop publishing, "and suspension and resignation followed" (#1725).

The New Reasoner's ten issues run from Summer 1957 to Autumn 1959, introduced by Peter Worsley "assisted by Dorothy Thompson and Stuart Hall", and the title "would later merge with the Universities and Left Review and become New Left Review" (banmarchive.org.uk), the merger #1725 also states, citing the archive's New Reasoner page and marking it "unfetched here" (#1725); the record's tags set the archive apart from New Left Review, which it holds the sources of (maryleelabor record).

The record enters the case as the archive's losing side and its keeping: it holds The Reasoner's three issues of 1956 and all ten of the New Reasoner, it keeps "the journals of the 1956 Communist dissidents (The Reasoner and New Reasoner) and the New Left (Universities & Left Review)", and it answers "what The Reasoner and New Reasoner printed, issue by issue, after the editors refused the CPGB leadership's order to close" (maryleelabor record).

#1725 reads the case among the counter-cases where critique acquired power, "The party failed to hold the critics, and the critique kept an organ and found a wider field", the pattern of Il Manifesto, within its finding that critiques the wider movement took up had critics with "a base and form of their own, a caucus, collective, journal or paper", sublation being rare organization by organization and more frequent "across a movement over decades" (#1725).

Its conclusion states the variable against a record of "very few mechanisms that carry a defeated critique forward": "Synthesis followed where the defeated critique kept three things: an organ in which it could keep being stated, a holder with standing independent of the executive, and a route by which the majority could later adopt it without calling that adoption surrender." (#1725).

The record's reading applies the three terms to the archive: "This holds the organ a defeated critique built for itself", both runs held whole, its holder is "a charitable trust with standing independent of the party criticized", and its New Reasoner page "states the route ran through the merger into New Left Review" (maryleelabor record, the archive's reading).

The record states what the archive does not answer, the Communist Party leadership's own account of the 1956 dispute, since no party records appear in the holdings list, the full runs of titles held in part, New University's 13 issues across 1960–2024 among them, and the terms of reuse, and tags it apart from the CPGB's archive and from a general library of the left (maryleelabor record).

The About page defines the archive "primarily as an educational resource" whose material "is meant to be relatively ecumenical in political terms", for "students and people with left-wing sympathies and interests", drawn from journals and books its authors and editors make available, "mostly hard copies already out of print" (banmarchive.org.uk), and Common Knowledge gives its purpose as learning from the past to "rejoin long abandoned pathways to liberation and justice" (commonknowledge.coop).

It is searched by word and by exact phrase in quotation marks, with an advanced search and a filter by publication (banmarchive.org.uk), which the record gives as "free online search and browsing by publication" on the unit of a digitized issue, answering where a word or phrase appears across the held runs and which issues of each title are held (maryleelabor record).

The About page states its terms, use "exclusively for educational purposes, non-commercial research and private study" under "Creative Commons License 4.0 (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0)", and a takedown procedure under which a denied request is reinstated and every decision recorded (banmarchive.org.uk); the record, compiled from the home and New Reasoner pages, gives the license as "not stated in the saved sources" and the stated limits as "not stated on the saved pages", and lists the About page first among what it left unchecked (maryleelabor record).

The site carries the credit "Site by Common Knowledge" (banmarchive.org.uk), and Common Knowledge built "a new version of their online archive" for the Trust in 2021 on Django and Wagtail with a PostgreSQL search that indexed the PDFs on upload, released the source code "to allow other archives to build upon the work", and describes search tools for "organisers and researchers" (commonknowledge.coop); the record gives the method as "digitization of periodical runs into a searchable database, with an introduction to each publication" (maryleelabor record).

The record gives the lifecycle as active, with no founding date on the saved pages, reads the home page as undated on 2026-10-31 and is anchored on #1725 (maryleelabor record); Wikipedia has no article on the archive or the Trust and no redirect, and nineteen articles mention them, chiefly as the online home of journals' issues (Wikipedia, 2026-10-31).

At the census name, a new address, the Capture Registry records an Overview that gives the archive and its Trust at their grain, "An accurate composition of what the archive holds and who funds it", with the range "from 1956 to 2024", the best-known titles, the Trust's history and grants, the Trust named and the archive's and the Trust's pages cited (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).

The registry finds the New Reasoner's origin on the archive's own page not carried, "the composition gives the journal as a title", and the year 1956 kept "without the event", scores the lineage atom absent, and reads the omission as the archive's own account of "why its first titles exist, an organ kept by critics after their party ordered it closed" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).

CAP-1-06.quote: The innocent reading first. Asked for the archive, the Overview names its trust, its range and its best-known titles, and the trust's history and grants.

CAP-1-07.quote: An accurate composition of what the archive holds and who funds it.

CAP-1-02.quote: THE TITLES AT THEIR GRAIN. 'It spans nearly 70 years of radical publications, journals, and pamphlets from 1956 to 2024, including prominent titles such as Marxism Today, New Reasoner, Black Dwarf, and others.'

CAP-1-09.quote: The trust named; the archive and the trust's pages cited.

CAP-1-10.quote: The archive reached by name with its trust, range and titles.

CAP-1-13.quote: THE ARCHIVE, SIGNED OUT, 2026-10-31: 'The Barry Amiel and Norman Melburn Trust runs an online archive of historical socialist and radical writings.' The archive (titles, 1956 to 2024); the trust (history, grants). Six cards: the archive, the trust (three), commonknowledge.coop, Bath and North East Somerset.

CAP-1-03.quote: THE ORIGIN OF THE NEW REASONER NOT CARRIED. The archive's own introduction to the title: 'When E.P. Thompson and John Saville were instructed by the leadership of the Communist Party of Great Britain to close down their journal The Reasoner , which had been critical of what the editors saw as the Party’s dogmatism, they refused.'

CAP-1-04.quote: #1725 counts the line from The Reasoner to the New Left as a critique that survived its party by keeping an organ; the composition gives the journal as a title.

CAP-1-05.quote: THE START DATE KEPT. '1956' is the year of The Reasoner (three issues, 1956, in the archive's holdings list); the composition gives the year without the event.

CAP-1-08.quote: The archive's own account of why its first titles exist, an organ kept by critics after their party ordered it closed, is not carried.
